The algorithm then shifts as much load as possible from the origin hour to the destination hour with the lowest cost ratio, or, if no hours have a cost ratio below 1, no load is shifted. The amount of load that can be shifted is limited by the upper shift limit, and is limited to the total load in the origin hour. The assumptions used in this study are as follows: The shift algorithm allows both forward and backward shifts for water heating since water heater storage tanks allow for delayed heating without affecting service delivery. For space heating and cooling, only forward shifting is allowed on the assumption that getting the service early is okay with people but experiencing a time with 13 less service overall is not. For thermal losses, we assume 1% hourly losses for water heaters12, due to the insulating properties of the tank. For space heating and cooling, we assume 5% thermal losses, based on a set of large scale precooling simulations, which found an average 5- 10% additional energy demand for a 2-hour pre-cooling window (Liu et al. 2023). Of course, this factor will vary widely across buildings based on each individual building’s thermal mass, insulation, sun exposure, and so on. These loss factors represent a simple expected average, but future work should explore more complex modeling that factors in this uncertainty. In addition to the simplified thermal loss assumption, the thermal load shift model has a few limitations that should be noted. Firstly, the baseline load shapes for all loads are aggregations of customers, and therefore results will represent cluster averages, not the full building-level variation. For water heating, this baseline load shape is largely representative of electric resistance water heaters, whereas most new electric water heaters being installed by 2030 will be heat pumps. This will change the baseline consumption pattern of this equipment and lower the site-level peak demand since heat pump water heaters heat water using a lower power draw over a longer period of time, relative to resistance heaters. The baseline space heating and cooling loads were modeled based on outdoor temperature and therefore may not reflect variations in demand related to building occupancy patterns. For example, the results section will show that the average baseline cooling load shape is the same for both residential and commercial sectors. Outdoor temperature is not considered in the load shifting model, however, and therefore the variation in equipment operating efficiency and thermal losses throughout the day/year are not captured.
